source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Absolute judgment of one-dimension stimuli saturates at about 6.5 categories. This is a channel limit in bits, not a count of items.
numbers: Mean 2.6 bits, SD 0.6, range 3 to 15 categories. Pitch 2.5 bits (~6), loudness 2.3 (~5), salt 1.9 (~4), dot position in interval 3.25 bits.
quote: "it is only a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence."
limits: Pooled across subjects, so values are 'slightly too low' per Miller. Different labs and methods across the studies.
agent_relevance: Seven is not a fixed item count. Do not hard-code 7 as an agent budget.

source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Span is roughly constant in items, not in bits. Digits carry 3.3 bits each, words about 10 bits, yet span stays near 5 to 9.
numbers: Decimal digit span about 7 (about 23 bits); binary digit span about 9; monosyllabic word span about 5 (Hayes).
limits: Span in items drops as item information rises, so the 'constant 7' is only approximate. Miller says the generalization is tempting 'but not sound'.
agent_relevance: Capacity in items shrinks for heavier items. Weigh units by size, not by number of facts.

source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Recoding into chunks raises what is held. Smith's binary recoding experiment is Miller's evidence for chunking.
numbers: Spans 9 for binary digits and 7 for octal digits. Smith recoded 18 binary digits to 9 base-4 or 6 octal digits. Smith himself recalled 12 octal digits, so 24 to about 40 binary digits depending on grouping ratio (2:1 up to 5:1).
limits: One trained subject. Gains need a learned recoding rule; this is a practice effect, not a free lunch.
agent_relevance: A recoding scheme the agent already has (summary, schema label) can carry more than raw text, but only if the code is known in advance.

source: Cowan (2010) The magical mystery four: how is working memory capacity limited, and why?
finding: Central store holds about 3 to 5 meaningful items in young adults once rehearsal and grouping are blocked. Miller's 7 comes from strategies.
numbers: Estimates 3 to 5 chunks. Longer verbal chunks (idioms, sentences): only 3 or 4 recalled (Gilchrist, Cowan, Naveh-Benjamin 2008). Chen and Cowan: learned word pairs vs singletons both gave 3 to 5 chunks; with articulatory suppression about 3 units.
quote: "a central memory store limited to 3 to 5 meaningful items in young adults"
limits: Review, not a new experiment. Cowan is the leading advocate of the 4-limit, so rival views get less weight.
agent_relevance: The limit is about chunks, but a chunk is whatever is bound by prior learning. A well-formed schema unit could count as one chunk for the agent.

source: Cowan (2010) Magical mystery four, developmental and attention data
finding: Capacity differs by age and individual, and attention control is a separate factor. Capacity is not just processing speed.
numbers: Storage about 1.5 items in 7-year-olds vs about 3.0 in older children and adults (Cowan et al., in press). Saults and Cowan 2007: with sensory memory masked, about 4 squares; squares plus digits gave fewer squares but about 4 items total.
limits: Cross-sectional child data; estimates depend on the model used.
agent_relevance: Capacity is shared across modalities in the central store, so adding tool output of another type still competes for the same budget.

source: Cowan (2010) Magical mystery four, rival accounts
finding: Two rivals are named: controlled-attention (low span means storage filled with irrelevant items) and spread-thin resource views (no fixed item count).
numbers: Cowan argues storage differences exist beyond attention control. Rehearsal covers about 2 s of speech; running span still shows only the last 3 to 5 digits.
limits: Cowan's rebuttals are one side of the dispute; the discriminating tests (precision in change detection) are not opened here.
agent_relevance: If limits are resource-like, extra items degrade quality gradually. This matches LLM context behaviour better than a hard slot count.

source: Gobet and colleagues (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: Experts beat novices even on random material. This challenges a pure 'chunks need structure' reading of Chase and Simon.
numbers: 45 studies, 1,401 participants, 55 samples; meta-analysis on 24 studies, 903 participants, 28 effect sizes. r = .41, 95% CI [.29, .51], I2 = 63. Experts better in 49 of 55 samples. Trim-and-fill (publication bias) gives r = .29 [.17, .41].
limits: Moderate effect, publication bias present, heterogeneity high. Random positions may contain chance chunks, which chunk theory uses as an explanation.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage on shuffled input is smaller than on structured input, so context order matters. Order context to expose familiar units.

source: Gobet and colleagues (2017) random-material meta-analysis, domain moderator
finding: The random-material effect differs by domain, but the moderator is only marginal.
numbers: Music r = .69 (k = 5), games .42 (k = 11), programming .36 (k = 6), sports .30 (k = 3, CI includes 0), other .24 (k = 3). Q(4) = 8.69, p = .069. Presentation time had no effect: Q(1) = 0.89, p = .346.
limits: Music result may reflect less random stimuli. Few studies per cell.
agent_relevance: Programming experts, the closest to a coding agent, show a mid-size effect.

source: Gobet and colleagues (2017) random-material meta-analysis, Chase and Simon as original
finding: The original Chase and Simon (1973) study is tiny and is not in the meta-analysis. The robust chunking evidence comes from later work.
numbers: Chase and Simon 1973 appears with N = 3 and no skill effect recorded in the table. Gobet and Simon's earlier review of 13 studies found masters keep some advantage on random chess positions.
limits: The page did not give the original percent-correct figures; I did not read the 1973 paper itself.
agent_relevance: Do not rest the design on the famous chess figures. Rest it on the later larger meta-analyses.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: Training working memory, or learning music or chess, does not transfer broadly once active controls are used. Chunks are domain-specific, as chunking theory predicts.
numbers: Passive controls: music 0.25 SD [0.17, 0.34], k = 64; WM training 0.18 SD, k = 34. Active controls: music 0.03 SD [-0.07, 0.12], k = 54; WM training 0.05 SD [-0.05, 0.15], k = 40; chess 0.10 SD (one study).
limits: Effects in SD, not recall scores. Authors are chunking-theory proponents.
agent_relevance: Raising a general capacity is a dead end; gains come from domain chunks. Build task-specific schemas, not a bigger generic buffer.

source: Superbia-Guimaraes and Cowan (2026) The capacity of working memory for multiple, dissimilar sets of items
finding: Recall of one set of 3 items is limited by the number of sets as well as the total item count. Sets are stored as new, often incomplete chunks offloaded to activated long-term memory.
numbers: N = 181 across four experiments (Exp 1 N = 61). Trade-off: 2.77 items recalled from other sets per item lost from Set 1 with pauses (Exp 1); 1.44 when pauses were removed (Exp 3).
limits: Online samples; the benefit appears only with clear grouping cues (Exp 3 and 4). Offloading is not free: some of Set 1 is lost.
agent_relevance: Clear grouping boundaries and pauses between groups raise what is retained. Delimiting sections in the prompt is the analogue.

source: Musfeld and colleagues (2026) Revisiting Hebb: the mechanisms of repetition learning
finding: Repetition learning of a repeated list (the Hebb effect, a lab model of chunk formation) is argued not to be gradual and implicit as commonly claimed. Standard analyses were flawed.
numbers: Hebb 1961: nine-digit sequence repeated among fillers; recall of the repeated list rose with repetition while fillers stayed flat. The paper reanalyses earlier data with a corrected intercept and Bayes factors, and the conclusion changes.
limits: I read the abstract and opening only, not every reanalysis result. Reanalysis numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Chunk formation may be fast and often explicit, not slow. One clear restatement may build a usable unit.

source: Liu and colleagues (2025) Cognitive mechanisms underlying memory advantages in bridge experts
finding: Bridge experts' recall advantage depends on the hand being sorted by suit, not on rank order. Visual familiarity and abstract knowledge both contribute, so chunk/template and SEEK accounts are both supported.
numbers: Recall accuracy: group F(1,98) = 38.33, p < .001, partial eta2 = .281; suit categorization F(1,98) = 75.33, partial eta2 = .435; group x suit F(1,98) = 30.21, partial eta2 = .236. Experts had 10 to 30 years of bridge.
limits: The study cannot choose between chunking/template and SEEK.
agent_relevance: Familiar organization that matches a known template gives the benefit; random order gives much less.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo verbal and spatial n-back: sensitivity d-prime falls to about 1 at n = 3, similar to the human drop-off. The limit persists under feedback and chain-of-thought.
numbers: 50 blocks of 24 letters per n; 8 matches and 16 non-matches per block; temperature 1. Base, feedback and reasoning variants all have d' about 1 at n = 3; added noise lowers capacity further.
limits: Single main model; n-back is partly an attention task. GPT-4 tested only up to n = 3. Match to human data is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Even a good prompt does not remove tracking limits at about 3 items to update. Keep state updates small per step.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: Larger grid sizes raise spatial n-back capacity (less interference). Other 6B and 7B open models show very low capacity; GPT-4 is far higher.
numbers: Tested Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna-7B and 13B, GPT-4, GPT-3.5. Open models nearly indistinguishable and very low.
limits: No exact d' numbers extracted for the model comparison.
agent_relevance: Working-memory-like capacity scales with model quality, so the budget depends on the model chosen.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models (EMNLP)
finding: n-back d' rises with model size and instruction tuning; GPT-4 on 1-back in the 7x7 grid can match or exceed humans. Small models do better with simple answer-only prompts than with AutoCoT, PS or ToT.
numbers: Human d' 3.39 to 4.05 in the 4x4 grid. text-ada-001 and text-babbage-001 d' 0.01 to 2.51. Adding 'after thinking carefully, the answer is' lifted text-ada-001 to 25.4% (+15.8 points) on Tracking Shuffled Objects.
limits: Heuristic mapping from n-back to reasoning; authors admit n-back is not a pure measure. Old OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: Match scaffold weight to the model: heavy operators can overload a weak model.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models (EMNLP)
finding: A chunking prompt change worked on a tracking task. Attaching each person's ball colour to the name in one unit gave a large gain.
numbers: Tracking Shuffled Objects: text-davinci-002 reached 96.4%, a rise of 35.4 points over the original prompt. Code-style prompt gave +4.8 points on Web of Lies (96.4%).
limits: Prompt tuned on failure cases of the same benchmark, so possible overfitting to the task; one model.
agent_relevance: Supports a concrete operator: bind related facts into one unit, name(color), before asking for steps.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits, other cognitive-strategy prompts
finding: Authors also test rehearsal-style prompts (restating state each step) on counting and tracking, reporting gains. They state n-back results are heuristic for comparison.
numbers: See paper for per-task numbers; I extracted only the chunking and prompt-simplification ones.
limits: Gains came from manual prompt design, not an automatic method.
agent_relevance: Restating state each step is a cheap rehearsal operator the program can enforce.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive load limits in large language models: benchmarking multi-hop reasoning
finding: Irrelevant context degrades multi-hop accuracy in one model in a dose-response way, and length alone does not explain it.
numbers: Gemini-2.0-Flash: control 0.85, 20% irrelevant 0.82, 50% 0.78, 80% 0.72; slope -0.003 per % load (p < 0.001). Long-control 0.82 vs control, p = 0.45. GPT-4o: control 0.65, 80% load 0.55, p = 0.07. Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B: 0% in every condition. 10 replications x 200 questions.
limits: Preprint by an independent author; only one non-confounded model; GPT-4o had about 32% missing final answers; the 'seven chunks' framing is loose.
agent_relevance: Extraneous load costs accuracy even when length is fixed. Prune irrelevant context, do not just add budget.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Accuracy is U-shaped by position of the key passage: best at the start and end, worst in the middle.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA drops by more than 20 points in the middle; in 20 and 30 document settings it is below closed-book 56.1%. Oracle 88.3%. Claude-1.3 closed-book 48.3%, oracle 76.1%. 16K and 100K variants perform about the same when inputs fit both.
limits: 2023 models; later models reduce but may not remove the effect.
agent_relevance: Place the live goal and state at the start or end of the prompt, never buried.

source: Levy, Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same task, more tokens: the impact of input length on reasoning performance
finding: Reasoning accuracy falls with added padding at far below the maximum context, with the relevant facts held fixed.
numbers: Average accuracy across tested models fell from 0.92 to 0.68 at 3,000 tokens. Padding of different types and locations tested; next-word perplexity correlated negatively with reasoning score.
limits: Synthetic padding; each dataset shows different intensity.
agent_relevance: Longer context is not free even when relevant content is unchanged. Short prompts per step are safer.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: what's the real context size of your long-context language models?
finding: Near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack hides large drops on harder tasks like multi-hop tracing and aggregation as length grows.
numbers: 17 long-context models, 13 tasks. Only about half keep satisfactory performance at 32K even though all claim 32K or more.
limits: Synthetic tasks; threshold set against a Llama-2-7B reference.
agent_relevance: Claimed context window is not usable working capacity. Plan for an effective budget well below it.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context
finding: A single irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems sharply cuts accuracy. Self-consistency and an explicit instruction to ignore irrelevant text partly fix it.
numbers: GSM-IC built from GSM8K by adding one irrelevant sentence; tested Codex and GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003). Exact accuracy drops not extracted from the pages I read.
limits: Older models; mitigations only partial.
agent_relevance: Support for filtering before reasoning: instruct to ignore and strip off-topic text.

source: Feng and Steinhardt (2024) How do language models bind entities in context?
finding: Models bind entities to attributes with 'binding ID' vectors in a continuous subspace; discernability between IDs reflects distance, which suggests a soft capacity for how many entities can be kept apart.
numbers: Seen in every sufficiently large Pythia and LLaMA model tested. Causal intervention evidence. No capacity number given.
limits: Interpretability on open models and simple tasks; the capacity limit is an implication, not a measured count.
agent_relevance: Suggests entity tracking degrades smoothly with more entities, like a resource limit, not a hard 4.

source: Kim and Schuster (2023) Entity tracking in language models
finding: Tracking box contents through a series of operations works only in GPT-3.5 models pretrained on code. Text-only pretraining did not give it. Performance falls as operations increase.
numbers: Tested Flan-T5, GPT-3, GPT-3.5. Only code-pretrained GPT-3.5 tracks well; finetuned T5 learns non-trivial tracking that degrades on harder splits.
limits: 2023 models; exact accuracy by number of operations not extracted.
agent_relevance: Structured, code-like state may carry more than prose. Keep state in a structured form.

source: Thalmann, Souza, Oberauer (2019) How does chunking help working memory?
finding: Tests whether chunking frees working memory capacity or only aids retrieval from long-term memory. Not read this session; paywalled.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Only the title was seen in a listing.
agent_relevance: Check before claiming chunks reduce load in working memory itself.

source: Norris and Kalm (2021) Chunking and data compression in verbal short-term memory
finding: Compression-based chunking model of verbal span. Not read this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Only the title was seen in a listing.
agent_relevance: Possible bridge to the compression and Kolmogorov subfields.

source: Ma, Husain, Bays (2014) Changing concepts of working memory
finding: Review arguing for resource models over fixed slots in visual working memory. Full text fetch failed; claim is from memory of the paper.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Resource view fits graded degradation in LLM contexts.

source: Gobet and Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four ... or is it two?
finding: Re-analysis of chess recall suggesting the number of chunks in expert recall may be nearer two than four. Known from the title only.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Only the title was seen in a listing.
agent_relevance: Chunk count depends on how a chunk is defined; do not set a budget in chunks without a definition.
